client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately because my boss just dumped two new projects on me with incredibly tight deadlines, on top of everything I was already juggling at the agency. I barely slept this week trying to figure out how I'm even going to manage all of it. Honestly, I'm not sure talking about it is going to change the fact that the work is still sitting there waiting for me.
therapist: That sounds genuinely exhausting — carrying that much pressure while running on so little sleep would wear anyone down. I also hear a bit of skepticism about whether this space can actually help, and that's a completely fair thing to voice. While we can't make the deadlines disappear, I'm wondering if we could explore together what's making this feel so unmanageable — sometimes that's where we find a little breathing room.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess part of what makes it feel so unmanageable is that I don't even know where to start — like every time I sit down to work, I just freeze and end up staring at my screen for an hour. And then I feel guilty for wasting that time, which makes the anxiety worse, and it just kind of spirals. I'm not sure "exploring" that is going to break the spiral, but I'll try.
therapist: That freeze-guilt-anxiety spiral is so real, and it actually has a name in CBT — it's a classic cycle where avoidance feeds the very anxiety that caused it in the first place. I appreciate you being willing to try, even with some doubt, because just naming that spiral is actually the first step toward interrupting it. Can I ask — when you imagine sitting down to start, what's the very first thought that tends to show up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: The first thought is usually something like "there's no way I can do all of this," and it feels less like a thought and more like a fact. It's like my brain just decides the situation is impossible before I've even opened a single document. I know that probably sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels completely true.
therapist: What you're describing — that thought feeling like a fact rather than just a thought — is actually one of the most important things we work with in CBT, and it has a name: cognitive fusion. It doesn't sound irrational at all, because in that moment your nervous system is genuinely convinced it's true. I'm curious — when you said it out loud just now, did hearing yourself say it shift anything, even slightly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, maybe a tiny bit — like there was a small gap between me and the thought when I said it out loud, instead of it just being this wall I was up against. But I'm worried that gap disappears the second I'm actually back at my desk with the deadlines staring me down. It's easy to see it more clearly here, but I don't know if that clarity will hold when I'm in the middle of it.
therapist: That small gap you noticed is actually really significant — it means the thought *can* be seen as a thought, even if just for a moment, and that's the very skill we build on. Your worry about it disappearing under pressure makes complete sense, and honestly, your voice sounds like it's carrying a lot of that tension even as you're reflecting on this. What if we worked on a small, concrete anchor — something you could use right at your desk — to help you recreate that gap in the moment when you need it most?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I'm open to hearing what you have in mind, but I'm a little skeptical about whether something "small and concrete" can really cut through that level of panic when I'm already spiraling. Like, I've tried deep breathing before and it just felt silly and didn't really stop the thoughts from racing. What kind of anchor are you actually talking about?
therapist: Your skepticism is completely valid — and I want to be honest that I'm not talking about deep breathing or anything that asks you to relax your way out of panic, because you're right that it often doesn't touch the thoughts. What I have in mind is something more like a quick cognitive interrupt — a single grounding question you ask yourself, like "what's the one smallest next action I could take in the next five minutes?" — not to solve everything, but just to give your brain a concrete foothold instead of the overwhelming whole. I'm also noticing you sound like there might be more frustration or urgency underneath your words than you're fully letting on — is there something about past attempts to cope that felt dismissive or unhelpful that I should know about?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, honestly there is more frustration underneath this than I've been letting on. I've talked to people before — a friend, even a previous therapist briefly — and it always felt like they were handing me a tool and sending me on my way, like "here, fixed." The question you're suggesting actually sounds less dismissive than what I've tried before, but I'm still worried it won't work when I'm staring at two massive projects and my brain is telling me I'm already failing.
therapist: Thank you for trusting me with that — being handed tools without feeling truly heard is a real wound, and it makes complete sense that you'd come in guarded. I want to be clear that my goal isn't to "fix" you and send you off; the question I suggested isn't a cure, it's something we'd practice and refine *together* based on what actually works for you. So with that in mind, would you be willing to try it right now with one of those two projects — just to see what happens when we test it in a low-stakes moment, before you're already in the spiral?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, I'll try it with one of the projects — the campaign brief that's due first. When I ask myself "what's the one smallest next action I could take in the next five minutes," I guess the honest answer is just opening the document and reading what I already have, which feels almost too small to matter. But I notice I'm already second-guessing it, like my brain is saying "that's not enough, you need to have the whole thing figured out now."
therapist: "Too small to matter" is actually your brain trying to pull you back into the all-or-nothing thinking that fuels the spiral — but opening the document *is* a real action, and it's exactly the right size. I notice you found the answer pretty quickly when you asked yourself the question, which tells me the clarity is more accessible than you thought, even now. What would it mean to just trust that one small step, and let "figuring out the whole thing" be tomorrow's problem?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It would mean tolerating this really uncomfortable feeling that I'm not doing enough, which honestly might be the hardest part of all of this. Like, intellectually I can see that one small step is better than freezing for an hour, but there's this voice that keeps saying my boss is expecting results and opening a document isn't a result. I think I could try it, but I'm not going to pretend that voice is going to go quiet easily.
therapist: You've just named something really central — that the hardest work isn't the task itself, it's tolerating the discomfort of feeling like it's not enough, and that takes real self-awareness to recognize. That critical voice about your boss's expectations sounds like it carries a lot of weight, and I'm curious where it learned that "small steps don't count" — is that a message that shows up in other areas of your life too, or does it feel specific to work?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It definitely shows up in other areas too — like even when I'm not at work, I have this constant low-level feeling that I'm not doing enough, not keeping up with people I care about, not being a good enough friend. It's kind of exhausting to realize that this voice isn't just about the deadlines, it's more like background noise I've been living with for a long time. I'm not sure if that makes it easier or harder to deal with, honestly.
therapist: What you just described — that constant hum of "not enough" across every part of your life — sounds genuinely exhausting to carry, and there's something both hard and important about recognizing it's bigger than just the deadlines. I notice as you said it, your voice got quieter, like the weight of that realization is settling in rather than just being talked about. That kind of long-standing voice often has deep roots, and while it makes things more complex, it also means that what we work on together could have a much wider impact than just getting through these two projects.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually hit harder than I expected, because part of me has been telling myself this is just a work stress thing and if I could get through these deadlines I'd be fine. But hearing you say it might have wider roots makes me feel a strange mix of relief and dread — relief that maybe there's an explanation for why I always feel this way, and dread because it sounds like a much bigger thing to untangle than I was prepared for. I guess I'm wondering if we can actually make a dent in something that's been there this long.
therapist: That mix of relief and dread makes complete sense, and I want to sit with both of those feelings rather than rush past them — because they're both telling you something true. Yes, we can absolutely make a dent in something this long-standing; in fact, people do it all the time, not by overhauling everything at once, but through exactly the kind of small moments of clarity you've already had today. I'm curious — which feels stronger right now, the relief or the dread?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
